We also propose an economical version of the $Q$-learning method that streamlines the policy evaluation (backward) step. The theoretical results are illustrated on a stochastic assignment problem and a short-horizon multi-armed bandit problem.
item.dc:creator: Andrzej Ruszczynski, Tiangang Zhang

item.title: Propagation of Chaos in Contextual Flow Maps
item.description: arXiv:2605.16747v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a quantitative statistical theory of transformers in the large-context regime by adopting the abstraction of contextual flow maps (CFMs): dynamical systems that evolve a distinguished token in the presence of a contextual measure across a stack of attention blocks. Within this framework, the finite-context model approximates an idealized infinite-context system in which the contextual measure is replaced by its underlying population, so that the context length $n$ becomes a statistical resource. Exploiting the McKean--Vlasov structure of the dynamics and the classical machinery of propagation of chaos, we establish a forward bound controlling the deviation between the finite- and infinite-context CFMs uniformly along depth, and a backward bound controlling the deviation between the corresponding training trajectories uniformly across iterations of online gradient descent. Both bounds achieve the optimal Wasserstein rate $n^{-1/d}$ for general CFMs and parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$ for a restricted class of CFMs that includes transformers as a special case. The analysis rests on a new Eulerian adjoint formulation of the loss gradient and stability estimates for the resulting forward--adjoint system, both of which may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Shi Chen, Zhengjiang Lin, Kaizhao Liu, Philippe Rigollet

item.title: A new perspective in linear Cauchy Elasticity: variational minimum principles for statics, dynamics, and heterogeneous materials
item.description: arXiv:2606.24782v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A variational minimum principle for linear elastodynamics of a possibly heterogeneous material without a stored energy function is developed. It involves a change of variables to dual fields, and results in a degenerate elliptic Euler-Lagrange system, even when the primal elastodynamics is hyperbolic. Uniqueness assertions for the dual dynamic and static problems and implications of the degenerate ellipticity are sketched. Some implications pertaining to heterogeneous materials and ones with indefinite elastic moduli are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Amit Acharya

item.title: Low-Rank Denoising for Predict-then-Optimize
item.description: arXiv:2609.15111v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A shortest-path decision is often made from edge costs that are only observed through noisy samples, such as the average of $m$ simulation replications. When the mean cost vectors of different instances lie near a $k$-dimensional subspace, projecting the averaged sample onto that subspace should remove noise. We make this precise. The mean squared error of any projection estimator splits exactly into a variance term and a bias term. The best projector is the positive eigenspace of $\Sigma_c - D/m$, where $\Sigma_c$ is the covariance of the true costs and $D$ is the noise covariance. For a rank-$k$ signal, the projection has the error of a sample mean with a factor $d/(\mu k)$ more replications, where $d$ is the number of edges and $\mu$ is an incoherence constant. For a signal that is only approximately low-rank, every rank-$k$ projection has an error floor, and the plain average wins beyond an explicit replication count. A margin bound shows that the chance of choosing a suboptimal path falls at the same improved rate. A projector learned from $n$ noisy instances loses at most an $O(d/n)$ term.
item.dc:creator: Henry Aldridge-Krawciw, Irene Aldridge

item.title: Sharp Convergence and Sample Complexity of Policy Mirror Descent for Average-Reward MDPs
item.description: arXiv:2610.04117v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Policy mirror descent (PMD) has a mature finite-time theory in discounted Markov decision processes (MDPs), but less is known in the average-reward setting, a more natural objective for many control applications. We give a finite-time, finite-sample analysis of PMD in ergodic average-reward MDPs built around a single master recursion that governs convergence for any critic, without external regularization. Its specializations yield linear rates for exact, inexact-tabular, and linear function approximation (LFA) updates. For exact PMD, the rate is tight in the worst case, and convergence can become superlinear. We complement these convergence results with critics whose end-to-end sample complexities improve the prior best policy-gradient dependence from $|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3$ to $|S|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3+|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^2$ in the tabular setting and from $|S||A|\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^5$ to $d\,t_{\mathrm{mix}}^3$ under LFA. Matching information-theoretic lower bounds establish that both critics are optimal up to logarithmic factors.
item.dc:creator: Enes Arda, Atilla Eryilmaz

item.title: A general recipe for data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for iterative algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2610.23570v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Most convergence guarantees for iterative stochastic algorithms are stated at a fixed iteration count and do not justify stopping at a data-dependent time. Recent anytime-valid envelopes do, but deterministic ones are typically too conservative for practical stopping, and existing data-adaptive ones are derived case-by-case, each concerned with a specific algorithm and a specific noise model and boundary construction. This paper provides a general recipe for sharp, data-adaptive anytime-valid envelopes for a large class of iterative algorithms. Our approach has two key steps: an optimization module derives a one-step recursion that performance measures of many such algorithms satisfy, reducing the error analysis to time-uniform concentration for predictably weighted sums of noise. Then, a statistical module ports the sub-$\psi$ condition to vector-valued processes, uniformly over predictable weights, and derives off-the-shelf boundaries via mixtures, stitching, and product betting martingales. Combining the two yields readymade envelopes for many iterative algoithms including but not limited to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), Oja's algorithm, temporal difference learning, Q-learning, and Bures-Wasserstein SGD, many with no prior data-adaptive anytime-valid guarantees. Specifically, for SGD, our framework recovers, often under weaker conditions, or significantly sharpens every existing envelope we are aware of. Our constructions come with explicit implementation details and are substantiated by numerical experiments.
item.dc:creator: Soham Bonnerjee, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.26843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop quantum algorithms for optimal control over a prescribed finite time interval (finite horizon), focusing on continuous-time linear-quadratic regulation (LQR). This foundational control problem often requires solving a nonlinear matrix Riccati equation, which can be costly for large systems and long control durations on conventional classical solvers. We instead work directly with the state-costate optimality equations, reformulating the LQR problem as a multiple-shooting linear system. Importantly, we prove a condition-number bound for the system that is independent of the horizon, under stabilizability and detectability assumptions. By incorporating the initial and final conditions into a single linear system, we can solve the subsequent linear system more efficiently with a quantum linear systems subroutine. For a given initial state, our quantum algorithms return classical estimates of the optimal cost and the optimal control inputs at a selected time, without constructing a Riccati solution operator. Given sparse-matrix block-encodings, an initial-state preparation oracle and a fixed number of control inputs, the query and gate complexities scale polylogarithmically with system size and control duration, provided that sparsity, relevant norms, and stability parameters are bounded. The dependence on the target error is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors. We establish the required bounds uniformly in system size and duration for a family of damped mass-spring chains with two endpoint controls. Numerical experiments support the analysis.
item.dc:creator: Xiajie Huang, Cristina \'Alvarez Yuste, Nikita Guseynov, Nana Liu, Javier Gonz\'alez-Conde

item.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
item.description: arXiv:2610.38496v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.
item.dc:creator: Perceval Beja-Battais (CB), Alain Grosset{\^e}te (CB), Nicolas Vayatis (CB)
